expectedText:
EMPLOYEE NON-SOLICITATION AGREEMENT
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

RESTRICTION
For 12 months after Jordan Lee's employment with Acme, Inc. ends, Jordan Lee will not solicit or induce, or attempt to solicit or induce, any employee of Acme, Inc. to leave their employment.

A GENUINELY UNSETTLED QUESTION IN SOME STATES
Whether a restriction like this one — barring solicitation of a former employer's own employees, as opposed to its customers — can be enforced at all is a real, unresolved question in at least one state. California courts have gone different ways on it.

[Verified — checked 2026-08-30]
  "We hold that this contract, as construed, is not void on its face under Business and Professions Code section 16600."
  — Loral Corp. v. Moyes, 174 Cal. App. 3d 268 (1985) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2140771/loral-corp-v-moyes/)
  "We thus doubt the continuing viability of Moyes post-Edwards."
  — AMN Healthcare, Inc. v. Aya Healthcare Services, Inc., 28 Cal. App. 5th 923 (2018) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/4326974/amn-healthcare-inc-v-aya-healthcare-services-inc/)
  "We thus independently conclude section 3.2 of the CNDA is void under section 16600."
  — AMN Healthcare, Inc. v. Aya Healthcare Services, Inc., 28 Cal. App. 5th 923 (2018) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/4326974/amn-healthcare-inc-v-aya-healthcare-services-inc/)
  Known gap: In 1985, a California appellate court upheld a similar no-raiding restriction against a former executive as valid, reasoning it only slightly restrained trade. In 2018, a different panel of the same court, applying the California Supreme Court's intervening decision in Edwards v. Arthur Andersen, expressly doubted that the 1985 case remained good law, and held a similar restriction void as applied to individuals whose own profession was recruiting other people's employees. This is one state's real, citable split as evidence such uncertainty exists — not a claim about which state's law governs this specific agreement, or about how a court would rule on a different set of facts than either of these two cases.

THIS IS DIFFERENT FROM A CUSTOMER NON-SOLICITATION CLAUSE
A restriction on soliciting a former employer's customers is a separate question from the employee-solicitation restriction above, and in at least one state, better settled: a court there won't directly enforce a contract clause banning a former employee from soliciting former customers, though it can still stop someone from using the former employer's trade secrets to do so.

[Verified — checked 2026-08-30]
  "specifically enforcing . . . a contractual clause purporting to ban a former employee from soliciting former customers to transfer their business away from the former employer to the employee's new business, but a court may enjoin tortious conduct ... by banning the former employee from using trade secret information to identify existing customers, to facilitate the solicitation of such customers, or to otherwise unfairly compete with the former employer."
  — AMN Healthcare, Inc. v. Aya Healthcare Services, Inc., 28 Cal. App. 5th 923 (2018), quoting The Retirement Group v. Galante, 176 Cal. App. 4th 1226 (2009) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/4326974/amn-healthcare-inc-v-aya-healthcare-services-inc/)
  "unless they are necessary to protect the employer's trade secrets"
  — Muggill v. Reuben H. Donnelley Corp., 62 Cal. 2d 239, 242 (1965), quoted in Loral Corp. v. Moyes, 174 Cal. App. 3d 268, 275-76 (1985) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2140771/loral-corp-v-moyes/)
  Known gap: This means the underlying conduct — misusing confidential information or trade secrets to go after a former employer's customers — can still be restrained through trade-secret and unfair-competition law even where the contract clause itself can't be enforced directly. The Non-Disclosure Agreement document in this set covers trade-secret obligations separately; this document doesn't restate them.

NO "NARROW-RESTRAINT" EXCEPTION UNDER SECTION 16600
Section 16600 directs that it be read broadly, with no carve-out for a restriction that limits only a small or "narrow" slice of someone's business, trade, or profession. California's Court of Appeal has explained that this reflects the state Supreme Court's own refusal, in Edwards v. Arthur Andersen LLP, to adopt a judicially created "narrow-restraint" exception that a federal appeals court had recognized for a restraint covering only a small or limited part of a person's business, trade, or profession. Applying that rule, the same Court of Appeal held a contractual non-solicitation restriction void under Section 16600 even though the restriction could be characterized as narrow or limited in scope.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "This section shall be read broadly, in accordance with Edwards v. Arthur Andersen LLP (2008) 44 Cal.4th 937, to void the application of any noncompete agreement in an employment context, or any noncompete clause in an employment contract, no matter how narrowly tailored, that does not satisfy an exception in this chapter."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16600(b)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Business and Professions Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=16600.)
  "Our conclusion is further buttressed by the Edwards court's refusal to adopt the "limited or 'narrow-restraint' exception to section 16600" created by the Ninth Circuit in Campbell v. Trustees of Leland Stanford Jr. Univ. (9th Cir. 1987) 817 F.2d 499 (Campbell)"
  — AMN Healthcare, Inc. v. Aya Healthcare Services, Inc., 28 Cal. App. 5th 923 (2018), certified-for-publication opinion, official court PDF (https://www.courts.ca.gov/opinions/documents/D071924.PDF)
  "California courts have not embraced the Ninth Circuit's narrow-restraint exception"
  — Edwards v. Arthur Andersen LLP, as quoted in AMN Healthcare, Inc. v. Aya Healthcare Services, Inc. (see gap field on sourcing), 44 Cal. 4th 937, 949 (2008), quoted at 28 Cal. App. 5th 923 (2018) (https://www.courts.ca.gov/opinions/documents/D071924.PDF)
  "If enforced, section 3.2 thus restrained individual defendants from engaging in their chosen profession, even in a "narrow" manner or a "limited" way."
  — AMN Healthcare, Inc. v. Aya Healthcare Services, Inc., 28 Cal. App. 5th 923 (2018), certified-for-publication opinion, official court PDF (https://www.courts.ca.gov/opinions/documents/D071924.PDF)
  Known gap: Source independence: the statutory quote below was independently fetched from California Legislative Information (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov) and confirmed byte-identical across two fetches with two different User-Agent strings. The case-law quotes below were independently fetched from the official, certified-for-publication opinion PDF hosted on the California Courts website (courts.ca.gov/opinions/documents/D071924.PDF) -- a primary court source, not a mirror -- and likewise confirmed byte-identical across two fetches with two different User-Agent strings; this is the same opinion the corpus already cites elsewhere as 'AMN Healthcare, Inc. v. Aya Healthcare Services, Inc.' Real limitation on sourcing: the two quotations attributed to Edwards v. Arthur Andersen LLP itself were not independently fetched from Edwards's own opinion text. CourtListener's API was rate-limited (125 requests/day, already exhausted) and its opinion pages return an AWS WAF bot challenge rather than content; Justia and FindLaw mirror pages returned a Cloudflare bot-challenge page rather than the opinion; the California Courts website's own opinion archive does not retain a 2008 opinion (its D071924 PDF above is retained, but an equivalent S147190 URL for Edwards returns 404). Those two Edwards quotations are therefore reproduced only as block-quoted within AMN Healthcare's verified opinion text, not confirmed against Edwards's own opinion independently -- a meaningfully weaker form of verification than the AMN Healthcare and statutory quotes, which is why the case field for those two citations names the chain explicitly rather than citing Edwards alone. What this clause does not cover: AMN Healthcare's own facts and its own application of this no-narrow-restraint rule concerned a clause barring former employees from soliciting the company's other employees (travel nurses) -- the clause discussed in this document's clause on that split of authority -- not a clause barring solicitation of the company's customers. The customer-solicitation-specific rule (that a court will not directly enforce such a clause, though it may still restrain trade-secret misuse) traces to a different, earlier case, The Retirement Group v. Galante (2009), which AMN Healthcare quotes approvingly elsewhere in the same opinion -- see this document's clause distinguishing customer non-solicitation -- but which this clause does not independently verify by name against a fetched copy of Galante's own opinion; the California Courts archive did not have a retrievable PDF for that 2009 case either. This clause states the broader, general anti-narrow-restraint principle that both the employee-solicitation and customer-solicitation lines of authority are built on; it doesn't independently confirm that Galante's own reasoning used the term "narrow restraint," only that AMN Healthcare's use of that term arose in the employee-solicitation context. Left open: whether this rule applies identically where the person bound is an independent contractor rather than an employee, and whether it applies identically to soliciting prospective customers as opposed to existing ones -- neither question is addressed in the sources fetched for this clause.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT
Please sign below to indicate agreement to these terms.

Employee: Jordan Lee
Date: _______________
